dryRun.title: Adding 1,000 list items
rows: append each item to the live list
up to 1,000 layout passes if you read layout in between
build in a DocumentFragment, append once
read offsetHeight, write style, read again…
forced sync layout each time ("layout thrashing")
dryRun.note: Changing the DOM is cheap; making the browser recalculate layout is not. Reading a layout value (offsetHeight, getBoundingClientRect) right after a write forces a reflow. Batch reads first, then writes, and insert many nodes at once. Use textContent for user text: innerHTML runs it as HTML.

think.q: You show a user's comment on the page. Which is safe?
why: textContent never parses HTML, so a comment like <img onerror=…> is shown as text, not executed.

think.q: for (const el of items) { el.style.width = box.offsetWidth + "px" } is slow. Why?
opts: Each loop reads offsetWidth after a style write, forcing a fresh layout every time
why: Read offsetWidth once before the loop, then only write in the loop.

think.q: What does appending a DocumentFragment do?
opts: Moves all its children into the target in one insertion; the fragment itself is not added
why: One insertion means one layout instead of many.

think.q: Changing which property usually avoids layout and only triggers compositing?
why: transform and opacity can be animated on the compositor; geometry changes need layout.

think.q: const items = document.getElementsByClassName("x"), then you remove one element with that class. What happens to items.length?
opts: It drops by one: getElementsByClassName returns a live collection
why: querySelectorAll returns a static NodeList; getElementsBy* return live collections.

try.task: Write renderList(items) that returns an HTML string <ul><li>…</li>…</ul> for an array of strings, escaping &, <, >, " and ' so user text can never become HTML.
try.hint: Replace & first, then the others. Build the whole string and assign innerHTML once.

takeaway.key: Batch DOM reads before writes, insert many nodes at once, animate transform/opacity, and use textContent for user text.
mistakes: Reading layout inside a loop that writes styles.

dryRun.title: Click on <span> inside <button data-id="7"> inside <ul id="list">
dryRun.note: Events bubble up from the clicked element. Delegation = one listener on a parent that handles clicks for all children, current and future, using e.target.closest(selector). Fewer listeners, and dynamically added items just work.

think.q: A listener on ul fires for a click on an li inside it. What are e.target and e.currentTarget?
opts: target = li (what was clicked), currentTarget = ul (where the listener is)
why: currentTarget is always the element the listener is attached to.

think.q: The li contains an icon <svg>. Clicking the icon gives e.target = svg. How do you get the li?
why: closest walks up to the nearest matching ancestor (or itself), whatever was clicked inside.

think.q: What does e.stopPropagation() in the li handler do to a delegated listener on ul?
opts: The ul listener never sees the click
why: It stops bubbling. preventDefault is the one that stops the default action (like following a link).

think.q: Which event does NOT bubble, so it needs focusin or capture for delegation?
why: focus/blur do not bubble; focusin/focusout do.

think.q: A table gets 500 rows added by fetch after load. Why delegation?
opts: One listener on the table handles all rows, including rows added later
why: No need to attach (and later remove) 500 listeners.

try.task: Implement delegation without a browser. Nodes are plain objects { tag, id?, parent }. Write closest(node, tag, root): walk up from node (inclusive) and return the first node with that tag, stopping (null) once you pass root. Then delegate(root, tag, handler) returns a listener (event) => … that calls handler(match, event) only when closest finds a match.
try.hint: Loop: while (n) { if (n.tag === tag) return n; if (n === root) return null; n = n.parent }.

checks.verify: const ul = { tag: "ul" }, b = { tag: "button", id: 7, parent: ul }, s = { tag: "span", parent: b }; assert(closest(s, "button", ul) === b && closest(b, "button", ul) === b, "closest")
const body = { tag: "button" }, ul = { tag: "ul", parent: body }, li = { tag: "li", parent: ul }; assert(closest(li, "button", ul) === null, "escaped root")

checks.t: delegate calls the handler only for matches
checks.verify: const ul = { tag: "ul" }, b = { tag: "button", id: 7, parent: ul }, s = { tag: "span", parent: b }, other = { tag: "p", parent: ul }; const got = []; const l = delegate(ul, "button", (m) => got.push(m.id)); l({ target: s }); l({ target: other }); assert(got.join() === "7", got.join())

takeaway.key: Events bubble; put one listener on a parent and use e.target.closest(selector) to find the item. Use focusin/capture for non-bubbling events.
mistakes: Using e.target directly when the click can land on a child element.

dryRun.title: const res = await fetch(url); const data = await res.json()
dryRun.note: fetch only rejects when no response arrives. An HTTP error is still a response: check res.ok (status 200–299). The body is a stream you can read once. Cancel or time out requests with an AbortController. XHR is the old callback API; fetch replaced it.

think.q:
const res = new Response('not found', { status: 404 })
console.log(res.ok, res.status)
why: 404 is a valid response, so fetch would resolve; ok is false because the status is not 2xx.
think.exec:
const res = new Response('not found', { status: 404 })
console.log(res.ok, res.status)

think.q:
const res = new Response('{"a":1}')
res.json().then(async (d) => { console.log(d.a); try { await res.json() } catch (e) { console.log(e.name) } })
why: The body stream is consumed once. Clone the response (res.clone()) if you need it twice.
think.exec:
const res = new Response('{"a":1}')
res.json().then(async (d) => { console.log(d.a); try { await res.json() } catch (e) { console.log(e.name) } })

think.q:
const ac = new AbortController()
const p = new Promise((_, reject) => ac.signal.addEventListener('abort', () => reject(ac.signal.reason)))
ac.abort()
p.catch((e) => console.log(e.name))
why: abort() rejects with an AbortError (a DOMException). fetch reacts to the signal the same way.

think.q:
const u = new URL('/api/users?page=2', 'https://example.com')
u.searchParams.set('q', 'a b&c')
console.log(u.href)
why: URLSearchParams encodes values for you. Never build query strings by hand.

think.q: Which fetch option sends cookies to a different origin?
why: Cross-origin cookies need credentials: "include" and the server must allow it (CORS with credentials).

try.task: Write fetchJson(url, { fetchImpl = fetch, timeoutMs = 5000 } = {}): call fetchImpl(url, { signal }), throw Error("HTTP " + status) when !res.ok, return parsed JSON, and abort with Error("timeout") after timeoutMs.
examples: await fetchJson("/x", { fetchImpl: async () => new Response('{"a":1}') })  // { a: 1 }
try.hint: Create an AbortController, setTimeout(() => ac.abort(), timeoutMs), and in catch turn an AbortError into Error("timeout"). Clear the timer in finally.

checks.verify: const d = await fetchJson("/x", { fetchImpl: async () => new Response('{"a":1}') }); assert(d && d.a === 1, "json")

checks.t: HTTP errors throw with the status
checks.verify: let e; try { await fetchJson("/x", { fetchImpl: async () => new Response("no", { status: 404 }) }) } catch (x) { e = x }; assert(e && e.message === "HTTP 404", "404")

const slow = (u, { signal }) => new Promise((res, rej) => signal.addEventListener("abort", () => rej(signal.reason))); let e; try { await fetchJson("/x", { fetchImpl: slow, timeoutMs: 20 }) } catch (x) { e = x }; assert(e && e.message === "timeout", "timeout")

takeaway.key: fetch rejects only on network failure: check res.ok. Read the body once. Use AbortController for timeouts and cancelling.
mistakes: Building query strings by hand instead of URLSearchParams.

dryRun.title: Where to keep data in the browser
dryRun.note: localStorage stores strings only (use JSON), is synchronous (blocks the main thread on big data) and shared by all tabs of the same origin. Never store tokens there if you can use an HttpOnly cookie: any XSS can read localStorage.

think.q: localStorage.setItem("n", 5); typeof localStorage.getItem("n") gives?
why: Everything is converted to a string. Objects become "[object Object]" unless you JSON.stringify them.

think.q: What does localStorage.getItem("nope") return?
why: getItem returns null for missing keys (unlike property access, which gives undefined).

think.q: Why is storing an auth token in localStorage risky?
opts: It is sent to every website
Any injected script (XSS) can read it; an HttpOnly cookie cannot be read by JS
why: Protect against XSS anyway; HttpOnly limits the damage.

think.q: Tab A changes localStorage. How can tab B react?
opts: Listen to the window "storage" event, which fires in other tabs of the same origin
why: The storage event fires in the other tabs, not the one that wrote.

think.q:
const data = { when: new Date(0), tags: new Set(['a']) }
const back = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(data))
console.log(typeof back.when, JSON.stringify(back.tags))
why: Saving through JSON turns Dates into strings and Sets into {}. Convert them yourself when saving and loading.

try.task: Write createStore(storage, ns) over any object with getItem/setItem/removeItem (localStorage in the browser). It returns { set(key, value, ttlMs?), get(key, fallback) }: values are JSON-encoded under ns:key, expired or corrupt entries return the fallback (and are removed).
examples: const s = createStore(localStorage, "app"); s.set("user", { id: 1 }); s.get("user").id  // 1
s.set("otp", "1234", 10); // after 10 ms: s.get("otp", null) → null
try.hint: Store { v, exp } as JSON. In get, JSON.parse inside try/catch; check exp against Date.now().

checks.verify: const m = new Map(); const st = { getItem: (k) => m.get(k) ?? null, setItem: (k, v) => m.set(k, String(v)), removeItem: (k) => m.delete(k) }; const s = createStore(st, "app"); s.set("user", { id: 1 }); assert(s.get("user").id === 1 && m.has("app:user"), "roundtrip")

const m = new Map(); const st = { getItem: (k) => m.get(k) ?? null, setItem: (k, v) => m.set(k, String(v)), removeItem: (k) => m.delete(k) }; const s = createStore(st, "a"); s.set("otp", "1", 10); await sleep(25); assert(s.get("otp", null) === null && !m.has("a:otp"), "ttl")

checks.t: corrupt or missing entries return the fallback
checks.verify: const m = new Map([["a:bad", "{oops"]]); const st = { getItem: (k) => m.get(k) ?? null, setItem: (k, v) => m.set(k, String(v)), removeItem: (k) => m.delete(k) }; const s = createStore(st, "a"); assert(s.get("bad", 7) === 7 && s.get("none", 8) === 8, "fallback")

takeaway.key: localStorage: strings only, synchronous, per origin, readable by any script. JSON-encode, handle corrupt data, and keep secrets in HttpOnly cookies.
mistakes: Trusting stored data to always parse.

dryRun.title: Caching strategies for a request
rows: HTML, API data that must be fresh
cache now, update cache in background
dryRun.note: A service worker is a script the browser runs between your page and the network. It intercepts fetch events and can answer from the Cache API, which makes offline apps and instant repeat loads possible. It needs HTTPS and has a lifecycle: install → waiting → activate.

think.q: You deploy a new service worker. Why do users still get the old one?
opts: Browsers cache it for a week
The page must call update() every time
The new worker waits until all tabs using the old one are closed (unless you call skipWaiting)
why: That waiting step protects open tabs from a mid-session switch.

think.q: A service worker at /app/sw.js controls which pages by default?
why: Scope is the folder of the script unless a header allows wider.

think.q: Which strategy fits an HTML page that must show the latest content when online but still open offline?
opts: Network first, falling back to cache
why: Fresh when possible, available when not.

think.q: Can a service worker change the page's DOM directly?
opts: No: it has no DOM; it talks to pages with postMessage
why: Like Web Workers, service workers run without a document.

think.q:
const cache = new Map()
const put = (url, body) => cache.set(url, body)
put('/a.js', 'v1')
const hit = cache.get('/a.js') ?? 'network'
const miss = cache.get('/b.js') ?? 'network'
console.log(hit, miss)
why: Cache first in miniature: answer from the cache when present, go to the network only for misses.

try.task: Write the two core strategies over injected helpers (so they run anywhere): cacheFirst(url, cache, fetchImpl) returns the cached value or fetches, stores and returns it; staleWhileRevalidate(url, cache, fetchImpl) returns the cached value at once (if any) but always refreshes the cache in the background. cache is a Map.
examples: await cacheFirst("/a", new Map([["/a", "old"]]), fetchFn)  // "old", no fetch
await staleWhileRevalidate("/a", cache, fetchFn)  // "old" now, cache becomes "new"
try.hint: cacheFirst: if (cache.has(url)) return it. SWR: start const p = fetchImpl(url).then(v => (cache.set(url, v), v)); return cache.has(url) ? cache.get(url) : p.

checks.t: cacheFirst uses the cache without fetching
checks.verify: let n = 0; const v = await cacheFirst("/a", new Map([["/a", "old"]]), async () => (n++, "new")); assert(v === "old" && n === 0, "hit")

checks.t: cacheFirst fetches and stores on a miss
checks.verify: const c = new Map(); const v = await cacheFirst("/a", c, async () => "new"); assert(v === "new" && c.get("/a") === "new", "miss")
const c = new Map([["/a", "old"]]); const v = await staleWhileRevalidate("/a", c, async () => "new"); await sleep(5); assert(v === "old" && c.get("/a") === "new", "swr")

takeaway.key: A service worker intercepts requests and answers from the Cache API. Pick a strategy per resource: cache first for static assets, network first for fresh content, SWR for "good enough now".
mistakes: Caching HTML cache-first and never seeing updates.
Forgetting that a new worker waits until old tabs close.
